overview.summary: New Zealand construction includes residential and non-residential building, civil infrastructure, specialist trades, maintenance and fit-out. Demand is project-based and regionally uneven. A visible pipeline can support revenue, but profit and cash depend on bid discipline, contract terms, delivery performance, subcontractor capacity, variations, retentions and the timing mismatch between progress claims and project expenditure.
business_models: Main contractors delivering fixed-price, cost-reimbursable, design-and-build or negotiated projects
Residential builders delivering contracted homes, developments or alterations
Civil contractors performing earthworks, roading, drainage, utilities and infrastructure maintenance
Specialist subcontractors supplying labour, materials and technical installation
Maintenance and facilities contractors earning recurring or schedule-of-rates revenue
industry_structure: The industry is fragmented, with a small group of larger contractors and many regional builders and specialist trades.
Projects often rely on multi-tier subcontracting, creating shared delivery and counterparty risk.
Public infrastructure, private development and housing cycles have different procurement and funding characteristics.
demand_drivers: Residential consenting, household confidence, mortgage conditions and population growth
Commercial development economics, vacancy, rents and investor funding
Central and local government infrastructure programmes
Repair, maintenance, seismic, weather-resilience and compliance work
margin_and_cost_drivers: Tender discipline, contingency, escalation clauses and accuracy of labour and material estimates
Variation approval, delay damages, rework, defects and subcontractor performance
Site supervision, labour availability, productivity and plant utilisation
Material prices, procurement lead times, insurance, bonds and finance costs
cyclicality_and_seasonality: New-build activity is cyclical and responds to finance availability and client confidence.
Weather, holiday shutdowns and consent or design delays can shift revenue and working capital between periods.
Maintenance and public infrastructure may be more defensive but are still exposed to procurement cycles and budgets.
overview.working_capital_profile: Construction cash flow can diverge sharply from reported profit. Progress claims are paid after work is performed; retentions, uncertified variations, disputed claims and work in progress can lock up cash, while suppliers and wages fall due earlier. Advance payments and favourable terms can temporarily flatter liquidity and should be separated from sustainable working capital.
overview.asset_intensity: Main building contractors may own relatively little plant but require bonds, guarantees and working capital. Civil contractors can be plant-intensive. Specialist trades vary. Work in progress, retentions and receivables may be economically important but are less reliable collateral than cash or unencumbered equipment.
regulatory_and_compliance: Building Act, Building Code, consenting, licensed building practitioner and trade-certification requirements
Construction Contracts Act payment, adjudication and retention-money obligations
Health and Safety at Work duties across overlapping PCBUs and sites
Resource, environmental, insurance, bonding and procurement conditions relevant to each project

subsectors.name: Residential building
subsectors.business_model: Contract homes, alterations or developer-led housing are delivered through staged progress payments.
subsectors.working_capital: Deposits may help early cash flow, but stage-claim timing, client finance and defects can create sharp gaps.
subsectors.asset_intensity: Usually modest plant ownership but high working-capital and guarantee exposure.

subsectors.name: Commercial main contracting
subsectors.business_model: Larger projects are managed under tendered or negotiated contracts using extensive subcontracting.
subsectors.working_capital: Retentions, claims and variations can be material; one disputed project can dominate liquidity.
subsectors.asset_intensity: Low-to-moderate physical assets but material contingent liabilities and bonding capacity.
valuation_watchpoints: Claims not booked as maintainable earnings

subsectors.name: Civil and infrastructure contracting
subsectors.business_model: Roading, earthworks, utilities and maintenance are delivered under projects or longer-term framework contracts.
subsectors.working_capital: Mobilisation and plant costs precede certified claims; public-sector clients can improve counterparty quality but not timing.
subsectors.asset_intensity: High where heavy plant is owned; replacement and utilisation are key.

subsectors.name: Specialist trades and building services
subsectors.business_model: Specialist labour and materials are supplied to main contractors or directly to asset owners.
subsectors.working_capital: Exposure to main-contractor payment, retentions and variation approval can be significant.
subsectors.asset_intensity: Usually lower than civil construction, with vehicles, tools and working capital.

primary_risks.mechanism: Under-pricing, escalation, delay, rework or subcontractor failure can turn a profitable contract into a cash loss.
Retentions, uncertified variations and slow certification consume liquidity and may be disputed.
Backlog can be delayed, cancelled or unprofitable, especially if the client lacks committed funding.
Bonds, guarantees, defects, retention trusts and subcontractor insolvency can create calls beyond booked debt.

cash_conversion_and_working_capital: Reconcile project ledgers, WIP, billings, receivables, retentions and cash received.
Age certified and uncertified claims separately and exclude speculative claims from liquidity.
Stress a major project delay while wages, subcontractors and plant costs continue.
Identify whether current cash is protected retention money or customer advances rather than free liquidity.
collateral_considerations: Plant needs ownership, prior-security and current forced-sale evidence; utilisation and specialisation affect value.
Receivables may be subject to set-off, defects, certification and counterclaims.
WIP and uncertified variations should receive conservative or nil collateral value.
Guarantees, bonds and retention obligations need to be included in the total contingent exposure.
downside_stresses: Gross-margin reduction on the largest live project
Three-month delay in certification and collection
Cancellation or deferral of a material portion of unsecured pipeline
Subcontractor failure plus remediation and replacement cost
monitoring_kpis: Backlog by status, client, completion date and forecast margin
Project gross margin and cost-to-complete variance
WIP, retentions, claims and receivable aging
Tender win rate and bid margin
Liquidity, net leverage, DSCR and bonding headroom
Health and safety, defects and disputes
covenant_considerations: Maximum leverage and minimum DSCR calculated after recognised project losses
Limits or reporting triggers for related developments, guarantees and major disputes
Monthly project, WIP, retention and pipeline reporting
diligence_questions: Which backlog is contracted, client-funded and supported by an approved budget and programme?
What are the latest forecast margin and cost-to-complete for each material project?
How much is tied up in retentions, uncertified variations, disputed claims and overdue receivables?
What bonds, guarantees, defects and retention-money obligations exist?
Which key estimators, project managers and qualified staff are required to deliver the plan?

value_drivers: Quality, diversity and margin credibility of contracted backlog
Disciplined estimating, project controls and early recognition of losses
Skilled management and delivery capability beyond the owner
Strong cash conversion and conservative claims accounting
multiple_influences: Maintenance-heavy, diversified contractors with repeat clients generally have more predictable earnings than project-concentrated new-build firms.
Backlog is valuable only where funding, terms, delivery capacity and forecast margin are credible.
Contingent liabilities, aggressive WIP recognition, plant catch-up and owner estimating dependence reduce transferability.
normalisation_focus: Project losses and claims based on latest cost-to-complete rather than historic margin
Owner estimating, project management and sales remuneration at replacement cost
Sustainable plant replacement and lease treatment
Related-party property, plant or subcontract arrangements at market terms
One-off disputes only when exposure is resolved and non-recurring
peer_selection: Separate residential, commercial main contracting, civil and specialist trades.
Match project duration, maintenance mix, contract form, plant intensity, scale and geography.
Compare cash conversion, claims policy, concentration and bonding needs before relying on observed multiples.
preferred_metrics: Price-to-earnings or DCF where debt and working-capital policy are aligned
Free cash flow after working-capital and maintenance capex
discount_and_premium_factors: Premium indicators include recurring maintenance, diverse funded backlog, strong controls and management depth.
Discount indicators include disputed WIP, project concentration, thin liquidity, contingent claims and aggressive revenue recognition.
diligence_questions: What portion of current EBITDA comes from favourable project timing or unapproved claims?
What losses emerge when every material project is reforecast independently?
How much working capital and bonding capacity must remain in the business after a sale?
Will client, subcontractor and qualified-staff relationships transfer?

market_research_sections.credit_paper:
Construction demand in New Zealand is spread across residential, non-residential and infrastructure work, with materially different regional and client cycles. MBIE's National Construction Pipeline provides a forward view of activity, but a favourable aggregate pipeline does not prove that a borrower's own backlog is contracted, funded or profitable. Lender analysis should distinguish secured work from preferred-bid and speculative pipeline, then test client quality, contract form, delivery capacity, concentration and the latest cost-to-complete.

The central credit issue is cash conversion. Progress claims follow expenditure, while retentions, uncertified variations, disputed claims and work in progress can absorb cash even where reported EBITDA is positive. Receivables may be subject to certification, set-off or defect claims, and protected retention money or customer advances are not necessarily available liquidity. Project-level margin, WIP and claim controls are therefore more informative than annual revenue alone. Bonds, guarantees, defects, related developments and subcontractor failure should be treated as contingent exposure.

The matched sub-sector changes the risk assessment: civil contractors may offer plant collateral but require replacement capex; main contractors may be physically asset-light but carry substantial project and guarantee exposure; specialist trades depend on qualified labour and main-contractor payment; residential builders are exposed to client finance and housing conditions. Conditions and covenants should address actual gaps in project reporting, liquidity and contingent exposure rather than assuming the sector pipeline is a mitigant.
market_research_sections.valuation_report:
Construction businesses should be valued on sustainable, cash-converting earnings rather than headline revenue or an untested order-book total. MBIE's pipeline research is useful for framing national and regional demand, while Stats NZ building-consent data can indicate prospective activity. Neither establishes the subject company's win rate, contract quality or margin. Backlog has value only when work is contracted, client-funded, deliverable within capacity and supported by a credible cost-to-complete forecast.

Normalisation requires a project-by-project view of margin, WIP, variations, retentions and claims. Favourable timing, front-loaded billings or unapproved claims can overstate maintainable profit; known losses should be recognised. Owner estimating and delivery roles require replacement remuneration, and plant-intensive contractors need sustainable replacement capex. Peer selection must distinguish residential building, commercial main contracting, civil infrastructure and specialist trades, then align maintenance mix, contract type, plant intensity, working-capital needs and concentration.

Transferable value is stronger where the business has recurring maintenance or framework work, disciplined bidding and project controls, diversified funded backlog, conservative accounting and management depth. Aggressive WIP, one-project concentration, thin liquidity, unresolved disputes, contingent guarantees and dependence on an owner-estimator warrant caution in forecasts and risk assessment. This sector baseline informs diligence; it does not supply a current transaction multiple.

limitations: National or regional pipeline forecasts do not establish the subject company's contracted backlog, funding, delivery capacity or profitability.
Project accounts, contracts, claims, retentions, bonds and latest cost-to-complete schedules are required for borrower-specific conclusions.
Construction conditions can change rapidly with finance availability, procurement and project delays; decision-date sources should be refreshed.
No current sector multiple is supplied and peer evidence must be matched to sub-sector, contract mix, capital intensity and cycle.
